summary: The order-service quote timeouts (INC-011) are caused by pricing-engine CPU saturation induced by the cfg-3120 feature-flag ramp: flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct was pushed from 5 to 100 at 12:04:00Z, after which all quote traffic ran through the expensive GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo calculator (paths=20000). CPU rose from ~40% to 98-99.5%, p99 jumped from ~60ms to ~2.6s, and quote budget overruns (2000ms) propagated to order-service's 2500ms client timeout. The reporter's suspicion of the market-data-service protobuf deploy is not supported: that service is flat/healthy across the whole window and its deploy at 11:56 precedes the 12:04 onset by 8 minutes. Confidence is medium (0.60) and the top hypothesis is clearly ahead of the alternatives, but sub-minute ordering of the flag change vs. the latency jump and the absence of GC/thread telemetry leave residual uncertainty.

ranked_hypotheses.title: GreeksV2 flag ramp to 100% made pricing-engine compute-bound (CPU saturation) → quote timeouts
ranked_hypotheses.statement: cfg-3120 ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 at 12:04:00Z, pushing all quote traffic through the expensive GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo calculator (paths=20000). The added compute load saturated pricing-engine CPU (~98-99.5% from 12:06 onward), slow calculations blew the 2000ms quote budget, p99 rose to ~2.6s, and order-service's 2500ms client timeout was exceeded, producing quote timeouts. Origin: pricing-engine config change (config_change), not the market-data-service serialization deploy.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-3120 ramps greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5 -> 100 at 12:04:00Z, sending essentially all quote traffic through the GreeksV2 calculator
GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo computations (paths=20000) take 6.5-8.9s, appearing first at 12:05:21Z
Compute load saturates pricing-engine CPU to a flat ~98-99.5% (max 100.0) from 12:06 onward
p99 latency jumps to 1705ms in the 12:04 bucket and holds ~2532-2746ms through 13:58
Requests blow the 2000ms quote budget: 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' from 12:06:41Z, ~12.5% 5xx
order-service's quote call times out after 2500ms, first error 12:06:10Z, 225 errors through 13:58

assumptions: The 12:04:00Z flag-change timestamp precedes (or is simultaneous with) the 12:04 p99/CPU jump; sub-minute ordering is unresolved (minute-granular flag timestamp vs bucket granularity).
The ~98-99.5% CPU is caused by GreeksV2 compute rather than GC pauses or thread saturation; no GC/thread/pool metrics were available (gap).
The remaining 5% of traffic pre-ramp plus 100% post-ramp is enough to raise CPU ~40% -> ~99% (i.e. GreeksV2 is dramatically more expensive than the default calculator).
cfg-3120 is the only relevant change to pricing-engine's behavior; no shared-library/infra change outside the deployment/config APIs coincided (dependency gap).

ranked_hypotheses.title: market-data-service protobuf serialization deploy (v5.2.0) introduced a costly/large quote payload that pricing-engine can't deserialize efficiently
ranked_hypotheses.statement: market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' deployed 11:56:00Z changed the quote payload format/size; pricing-engine's handling of that payload became slow or partially failing, degrading p99 and driving CPU on the pricing-engine path. Origin: market-data-service deployment (bad_deployment). This is the reporter's suspicion.

causal_chain.claim: market-data-service v5.2.0 switches quote serialization to protobuf at 11:56:00Z, 8 minutes before onset
pricing-engine consumes changed quote payloads on the market-data-service HTTP call path
Deserialization/parsing of the new payload is slow or fails, raising pricing-engine latency and CPU
quote budget (2000ms) exceeded and order-service 2500ms timeout tripped -> quote timeouts

assumptions: A serialization change can inflate pricing-engine compute/latency without changing market-data-service's own latency or CPU.
The absence of any serialization/deserialization error in pricing-engine logs is due to such errors not being logged verbatim.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Organic market-open/load-driven capacity saturation on pricing-engine (independent of any change)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Incoming quote volume on pricing-engine outgrew provisioned compute capacity, driving CPU to ~99% and p99 to ~2.6s, so order-service quote calls time out. Origin: pricing-engine capacity saturation with no faulty triggering change — matches historical precedent HIST-113. Origin: capacity_saturation.

causal_chain.claim: Quote request volume rises around 12:04 (market activity), approaching provisioned pricing-engine capacity
pricing-engine CPU saturates to ~98-99.5% (flat) from 12:06 onward
p99 latency rises to ~2.6s and stays there (no recovery)
order-service 2500ms quote calls time out, 225 errors 12:06-13:58

assumptions: Request volume increased organically; no request_rate data was retrieved to confirm a traffic surge.
The sustained ~99% CPU floor for ~2 hours is organic load rather than a change-induced constant-cost increase.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared-resource contention (redis-cache / ledger-db / kafka / shared node) degraded pricing-engine independently of the flag
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A shared component in the blast radius (redis-cache accessed by pricing-engine, ledger-db or kafka shared with order-service, or CPU contention on a shared node/namespace) degraded, pushing pricing-engine p99 over SLO and causing quote timeouts. Origin: shared dependency/infrastructure degradation rather than pricing-engine code or config.

causal_chain.claim: order-service and pricing-engine share ledger-db, kafka and redis-cache
A shared component (e.g. redis-cache cold-cache storm, or DB/broker pressure) begins degrading around 12:04
pricing-engine quote computations stall on the shared dependency, raising p99 and CPU
order-service quote calls exceed 2500ms -> quote timeouts

assumptions: A shared-dependency stall can raise pricing-engine own CPU to ~99% rather than idle-waiting.
No config-change record exists because the triggering event is organic degradation or infra-level.

facts.statement: pricing-engine p99 latency jumped from a stable ~58-61ms baseline to 1705ms in the 12:04 bucket and stayed at ~2532-2746ms through 13:58, i.e. ~2.6s ongoing and unrecovered.
pricing-engine HTTP 5xx error_rate rose from ~0.2% baseline to 4.47% in the 12:04 bucket and to ~12-13% from 12:07, holding ~12.5% through 13:58.
pricing-engine CPU saturation coincides with the latency jump: ~40% baseline, 68.44% (max 98.65) in the 12:04 bucket, then flat ~98-99.5% (max 100.0) from 12:06 onward.

pricing-engine logs show the earliest anomaly at 12:05:21Z with GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo computations (paths=20000) taking 6.5-8.9s, escalating into 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' errors from 12:06:41Z (342 slow-calc WARNs, 276 deadline-exceeded ERRORs total). The calculator in the error is GreeksV2, not a serialization path.

order-service's first ERROR is at 12:06:10Z; all 225 errors share the signature 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms' and span through 13:58:24Z, with no serialization/deserialization or 5xx errors logged by order-service itself.

market-data-service is flat/healthy across the incident: p99 steady ~38-43ms for the whole 11:40-13:58 window and CPU steady ~44-47% (max 49.97); its only log line in the window is an unrelated TLS-cipher WARN at 11:43:53Z.

The only deployment across all services in 11:30-13:59Z is market-data-service v5.2.0, 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf', deployed at 11:56:00Z (status live, never rolled back); there is no deployment for pricing-engine or order-service.

The only config/flag change in the window is pricing-engine cfg-3120, key 'flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct', changed 5 -> 100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z by pm-experiments ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic'), timestamped in the exact same bucket as the p99 and CPU jumps and matching the GreeksV2 calculator in pricing-engine's errors.
No config changes were found for order-service or redis-cache in 11:30-13:59Z, so no timeout/pool/TLS/DNS/resource-limit change is recorded for the callee chain or the shared cache.

order-service's dependency graph: it calls ledger-db (shared), pricing-engine (http), exchange-gateway (http) and produces to kafka (shared); pricing-engine calls market-data-service (http) and redis-cache (shared). Shared components in the blast radius are ledger-db, redis-cache and kafka.

Historical precedent HIST-113 (2026-01-28) 'pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open' had the same symptom pair (quote timeouts, cpu 99%) but was attributed to organic record market-open volume exceeding capacity.

Precedents HIST-101 (auth-service bcrypt cost 10->14 inside a release caused high CPU + p99/503s, resolved by rollback) and HIST-107 (redis-cache cold-cache storm caused quote latency) are leads only, not evidence of the current cause.

assumptions: Assumption: the 12:04:00Z flag-change timestamp precedes or is simultaneous with the 12:04 p99/CPU jump; sub-minute ordering is unresolved (minute-granular flag timestamp vs. bucket granularity).
Assumption: the ~98-99.5% CPU is caused by GreeksV2 compute rather than GC pauses or thread saturation; no GC/thread/pool metrics were available.
Assumption: the traffic mix shift from 5% to 100% GreeksV2 is sufficient to raise CPU from ~40% to ~99%, i.e. GreeksV2 is dramatically more expensive than the default calculator.
Assumption: cfg-3120 is the only relevant change to pricing-engine behavior; no shared-library or infra change outside the deployment/config APIs coincided with the 12:04 onset.
Assumption: pricing-engine is on the critical path for every order quote such that its degradation alone explains the order-service 2500ms timeouts (its errors are the same signature).

recommended_actions.action: Immediate mitigation: revert cfg-3120 by lowering flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 100 back to 5 (or 0) for pricing-engine, and watch pricing-engine CPU, p99 and order-service quote timeouts over the next 10-15 minutes.
recommended_actions.rationale: cfg-3120 is the only change coinciding exactly with the p99/CPU jump, and pricing-engine's own errors name calculator=GreeksV2 (F4, F8, F1, F3). HIST-101 shows a config-like cost regression inside a release was resolved by rollback (F12).

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back market-data-service v5.2.0 (dep-6111) as the first action; if a rollback is demanded for reassurance, note it is a low-probability lever and its deploy at 11:56 precedes onset by 8 minutes.
recommended_actions.rationale: market-data-service shows zero latency, CPU or error anomaly across the window, and the flag change is a far better temporal and log-content match (F6, F7, F4).

recommended_actions.action: Confirm the reversal: verify pricing-engine CPU returns toward ~40% baseline, p99 toward ~60ms and order-service quote timeouts cease; then close the incident and re-ramp the flag in graded steps (e.g. 5 -> 25 -> 50) with an explicit cost/latency gate.
recommended_actions.rationale: The whole incident signature is change-induced and ongoing (F1, F2, F3, F5); recovery on revert both confirms H1 and provides the fix path.

recommended_actions.action: Add a pre-ramp capacity/cost gate for pricing-engine flag experiments: estimate per-request compute for GreeksV2 (paths=20000) before ramping, and block ramps that would exceed headroom; alert on pricing-engine CPU > ~80% and quote-budget overruns.
recommended_actions.rationale: The root cause is a config ramp that ran the expensive calculator on 100% of traffic without a compute budget check; the same class of event (HIST-101) has occurred before (F4, F8, F12).

recommended_actions.action: Instrument pricing-engine with GC, thread-saturation and connection-pool metrics, and enrich the p99/CPU alerts so a compute-bound regression is distinguishable from GC or pool exhaustion.
recommended_actions.rationale: The CPU-saturation attribution rests on indirect evidence because no GC/thread/pool telemetry was available; this gap makes the conclusion harder to defend at second resolution (data gap; F3, F4).

recommended_actions.action: If discriminating is still needed, compare pricing-engine request_rate at 12:04 against the 11:30-13:59 baseline: organic-load saturation (H4) would show a volume surge, while a flag ramp should show roughly flat volume with a step change in per-request cost.
recommended_actions.rationale: Separates the change-induced compute hypothesis from HIST-113-style organic market-open capacity saturation, which shares the symptom pair (F11).

recommended_actions.action: Also check market-data-service error_rate and pricing-engine memory_pct for the onset window to close the outstanding telemetry gaps, and confirm whether order-service recorded any signal before 12:06:10Z.
recommended_actions.rationale: These queries were never executed due to call-budget exhaustion, limiting the strength of the alternative-hypothesis exclusions (data gaps; F5, F6).

data_gaps: market-data-service error_rate, order-service error_rate and pricing-engine memory_pct queries were never executed (call-budget exhausted), so order-service's own 5xx rate, market-data-service's error rate and pricing-engine's memory/GC trend around onset are unconfirmed.

No GC, thread-saturation or connection-pool metrics exist among the available metrics (cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts), so the ~98-99.5% CPU cannot be definitively attributed to GreeksV2 compute rather than GC pauses or thread saturation.

market-data-service INFO logs between 11:55 and 12:07 were not retrieved, so the reported serialization change could not be correlated to any log/metric event; whether it produced any telemetry is unverified.
order-service logs below WARN earlier than 12:06 and order-service metrics were not retrieved, so an earlier order-service signal before 12:06:10Z cannot be fully excluded.
No second historical search for a feature-flag-ramp CPU/latency precedent was possible (budget_exhausted), so the precedent set is limited to five incidents.

No shared-library/adapter artifacts, k8s resource-limit changes or CI/CD pipelines were inspected, so a change outside get_deployments/get_config_changes coinciding with the 12:04 onset is not fully excluded.
The exact sub-minute ordering of the 12:04:00Z flag change vs. the p99/CPU jump is unresolved (minute-granular timestamps).
One tool call (tc-002 get_config_changes by dependency) returned a PARTIAL result, so config-change coverage may be incomplete.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: pricing-engine request_rate showing a sharp, step-like surge at 12:04 with flat per-request cost would support H4 (organic capacity saturation, HIST-113 pattern) over the flag ramp.
Evidence that pricing-engine CPU/p99 remained elevated after reverting flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct to 5 would falsify H1 and reopen the investigation.
GC-pause or thread-saturation/pool-exhaustion evidence (e.g. long GC pauses, blocked thread counts) coinciding with the CPU jump would move the cause away from GreeksV2 compute.
Detection of a serialization/deserialization error, payload-size jump or latency change on the market-data-service protobuf path (or a market-data-service-side anomaly) would revive H2.
Discovery of a change outside the deployment/config APIs (shared library publish, k8s resource-limit change) timestamped at or just before 12:04 would reopen the space of triggering changes.
A confirmed, second-resolution ordering showing the p99/CPU jump strictly preceded the 12:04:00Z flag change would weaken the causal claim.
